title: Database and replica
subtitle: The school office’s official notebook and the photocopies around the school: quick to read, but always a little behind
mission: Enrollment week: the school office system gets 1,500 reads per second (report cards, timetables, records) and 100 writes per second. Each database server handles 1,000 operations per second. Writes always go to the main database (the primary); reads can go to replicas, which receive changes with a little delay. Ana saves her new phone number and reloads the page 300 ms later. Choose how many replicas to use and where the read right after a write comes from.

predict.question: each database handles 1,000 operations/s. With 1,500 reads/s, what’s the minimum number of read replicas so nobody goes unanswered?

options.one: 1 replica: it takes the reads off the primary
options.two: 2 replicas: the reads need to be split

feedback.right: right! With 1 replica, it gets 1,400 reads/s (the other 100 belong to people who just saved and go to the primary) and handles 1,000. With 2, each gets 700/s, 70% of capacity, and p95 drops to 50 ms. The table shows each case.
feedback.wrong: look at the table: with 1 replica, it gets 1,400 reads/s and handles 1,000, so it overflows. With 2, each gets 700/s. More replicas give headroom, but the minimum is 2.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run it and look at the replicas table.

coach.ui: guess noted. Run with 2 replicas and look at the table: it also shows 0, 1 and 3.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run replicate and look at the replicas table.

tryNext.ui: Now keep only 1 replica. Then go back to 2, read from the replica and lower the lag to 100 ms.
tryNext.cmd: Run replicate --replicas 1 and then replicate --read-after-write replica --lag 100.

why.simples:
The primary is the school office’s official notebook: only it receives changes, so there are never two notebooks disagreeing. Replicas are photocopies kept in other rooms. Lots of people can look things up at once and nobody has to line up at the office.
But the photocopy is updated afterwards: there’s a delay between writing in the notebook and the copy changing. For almost everything, that’s fine: the weekly timetable can be half a second behind. But if Ana just changed her phone number and goes to check, she needs to read the official notebook. Otherwise she sees the old number, thinks it didn’t save and saves again.
And notice: photocopies help readers. Writers still go to the same notebook.
why.dev:
In primary-replica replication, the primary writes every change to its log (in PostgreSQL, the WAL) and replicas apply that log. With asynchronous replication, the primary confirms the write without waiting for replicas, so they fall a little behind (the lag): milliseconds on a calm day, seconds or more under load or a bad network.
To avoid reading your own stale data (read-your-writes): send reads from whoever just wrote to the primary (for a few seconds, or within the same session), or read from the replica only after it has reached your write’s log position. Replicas don’t scale writes: that’s what partitioning (sharding) and queues are for. And track the lag (in PostgreSQL, the pg_stat_replication view shows replay_lag) with an alert.
why.especialista:
Synchronous replication removes the lag for confirmed writes (the primary waits for at least one replica to store them), but every write gets slower and, if the synchronous replica disappears, writes can stall: it’s a trade between durability, latency and availability. With asynchronous replication, a failover can lose the last confirmed writes that hadn’t reached the promoted replica yet.
Failover has its own traps: detecting the outage without false positives, promoting only one replica (avoiding two primaries, the split-brain), redirecting connections and rebuilding the old primary as a replica. Tools like Patroni and the cloud’s managed databases handle this. Other guarantees that matter to users: monotonic reads (not going back in time when switching replicas) and causal ordering. Also remember replicas don’t protect against human error: a wrong DELETE is faithfully replicated, so backups and point-in-time recovery are still needed.

steps:
Create a folder escola-banco with two files. replicacao.sh runs once, when the primary is created:
#!/bin/bash
# allow replication connections from the compose network
echo "host replication all all scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"

And the compose.yaml. The replica copies the primary with pg_basebackup (-R leaves it configured as a replica) and then starts in read-only mode:
name: escola-banco
services:
  primary:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: segredo
    volumes:
      - ./replicacao.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/replicacao.sh:ro
  replica:
    image: postgres:18
    user: postgres
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: segredo
    depends_on:
      - primary
    command:
      - bash
      - -c
      - |
        until pg_basebackup -h primary -U postgres -D /tmp/replica -R -X stream; do
          rm -rf /tmp/replica
          sleep 2
        done
        exec postgres -D /tmp/replica

Start it and wait for the replica to be ready:
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f replica
When database system is ready to accept read-only connections shows up, leave with Ctrl+C.

On the primary, see the connected replica and write some data:
docker compose exec primary psql -U postgres -c "SELECT client_addr, state FROM pg_stat_replication;"
docker compose exec primary psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE alunos (id int PRIMARY KEY, telefone text); INSERT INTO alunos VALUES (42, '15 99999-0000');"

On the replica, read the data and try to write:
docker compose exec replica psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM alunos;"
docker compose exec replica psql -U postgres -c "INSERT INTO alunos VALUES (43, '15 98888-0000');"
Shut everything down: docker compose down
recipe.ok: the primary’s pg_stat_replication shows one row with state streaming; the SELECT on the replica returns student 42; and the INSERT on the replica fails with ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction.
